claims.text: A model that decouples lattice and electronic heat transport will improve thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy for HfNbTaTiZr by roughly 20% relative to conventional combined models.
The intended samples are defect-controlled, well-characterized bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
The sample set includes oxygen-free material and material containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Lattice transport will be modeled using DFT-derived phonon properties and Debye-temperature estimates.
Electronic transport will be modeled using ab initio band structure and electron-scattering analyses.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Electronic heat conduction predominates in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
DFT-derived force constants, local disorder, and Debye temperature govern the relevant phonon dynamics and electronic band-structure properties.
Explicitly separating phonon dynamics from electron scattering reduces compounded uncertainty associated with integrated transport models.
Summing the separately predicted lattice and electronic conductivities will reduce prediction error by roughly 20% relative to conventional combined models.
The predicted lattice conductivity will agree with measurements below 200 K.
For oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr between 300 and 1200 K, predicted total conductivity will lie within 10–17 W/(K m).
Earlier predictive approaches conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Earlier predictive approaches typically have errors exceeding 20–30% across the stated temperature ranges.
The proposed approach is most reliable below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K for defect-controlled, near-equilibrium HfNbTaTiZr.
Model accuracy may diminish above 1200 K and for uncontrolled impurities or nonequilibrium microstructures.
Not all scattering channels associated with impurities and microstructural defects may be captured.
Electronic thermal conductivity can be inferred from resistivity using the Wiedemann–Franz law over 300–1200 K for the proposed comparison.
A deviation greater than ±20% in total conductivity or either separated contribution will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The central claim is a roughly 20% relative improvement over conventional models, but the falsification rule tests a ±20% absolute error without requiring comparison against a conventional-model error. Thus, passing the stated test would not establish the claimed relative improvement.

The entire region below 200 K is designated as an applicability regime and described as among the most reliable intervals, while the boundary also says accuracy may diminish at 'extreme low (<200 K)' temperatures without defining a narrower cutoff.
